title: String basics
description: Strings are immutable primitives — make them with literals or String(); read with .length and [i]; iterate with for...of.

notes: Prefer string literals over new String() — the wrapper object breaks === comparisons and has typeof "object".
Strings are immutable: s[0] = "X" does nothing; every transform returns a fresh string.
Out-of-bounds indexing returns undefined, not an error — guard with .length when iterating manually.

options: false — the wrapper object is not the primitive
true — `===` unwraps the String object before comparing
false — but `new String("hi") == "hi"` is also false
questions.explain: new String() creates an object wrapper; typeof is 'object'. Reference-equality against the primitive 'hi' is always false. Avoid new String().

questions.q: After `const s = "hi"; s.toUpperCase();` what is s?
options: undefined — the return value was discarded
"HI" — `.toUpperCase()` mutates in place when the receiver is a let/const

questions.q: Which loop iterates the CHARACTERS of a string?
options: for (const ch in s) — yields each character
for (const ch of s) — yields each character
for (let i = 0; i <= s.length; i++) — bracket-access in body
questions.explain: for-in returns string KEYS ('0','1',...), not values. forEach is array-only. The for-loop has an off-by-one (<= instead of <). for...of is the canonical char iterator.

exercises.prompt: Demonstrate immutability — assigning to s[0] is a no-op; .toUpperCase() returns a NEW string.
